usage: 에 marks where things exist; pairs with 있다/많다
N + 주변 = the surroundings of N, no 의 needed
을 marks what you scan with your eyes
주변 also covers the people in one's circle
examples: 호텔 주변에 식당이 많아요.
There are many restaurants around the hotel.
the everyday frame: N 주변에 + 있어요/많아요
역 주변을 한 바퀴 둘러봤어요.
I took a walk around the area near the station.
주변을 둘러보다 = scan/look around, object particle 을
여기 주변에 환전할 데가 있는지 좀 알려 주시겠어요?
Could you tell me if there's somewhere to exchange money nearby?
real travel ask — note polite 주시겠어요? softens the request
nuance: 주변 is Sino-Korean 周邊 ('encircling edge'), the zone wrapping around a fixed point — 'the area around X'. The near-synonym is 근처 (近處 'near place'): 근처 just means 'somewhere close by, in the vicinity', while 주변 implies the full ring of surroundings on every side, so 호텔 주변 feels like the whole neighborhood and 호텔 근처 feels like 'a spot near the hotel'. 주변 also stretches to people (주변 사람들 = those around you, your circle), which 근처 cannot do. It is neutral in register, fine in both speech and signage. The English-speaker trap is dropping the particle: 'restaurants around the hotel' tempts you to say 주변 식당 있어요, but to state existence you need 주변에 식당이 있어요 (에 = location). Also do not visually confuse it with 주말 (weekend) — same 주 but unrelated.

Using 주변 for one nearby spot. If you mean 'a place close by', 근처 is more natural (근처에 카페 있어요?); 주변 leans toward the whole encircling area.
Reading 주변 as 주말 (weekend) because both start with 주 — they share no meaning; 주변 = surroundings, 주말 = weekend.

usage: 에 marks the end-point as a location
N + 끝 = the far end/tip of N
all the way to the end
까지 = up to; 'to the very end' in space or effort
examples: 길 끝에 편의점이 있어요.
There's a convenience store at the end of the road.
길 끝에 = at the road's end, location 에
이 줄 맨 끝에 서시면 돼요.
You can stand at the very end of this line.
맨 끝 = the absolute end; -면 돼요 = 'it's fine if you...'
복도 끝까지 가서 오른쪽으로 도세요.
Go all the way to the end of the hallway and turn right.
끝까지 가다 + 오른쪽으로 돌다 = a real direction-giving line
nuance: 끝 is the native-Korean noun for the terminal point of something — the far tip of a line, road, or hallway, and by extension the end of a period of time (방학 끝, 여행 끝). Distinguish it from 가장자리 (the outer rim/edge of a flat thing like a table or page) and from 구석 (an inside corner where two walls meet): 끝 is the end of something long or linear, not a rim or a nook. Register is neutral and everyday. Two pitfalls for English speakers: spelling and the noun/verb split. The word ends in a single ㅌ (끝), often miswritten 끋 or 끝ㅌ; before a vowel that ㅌ links, so 끝에 sounds like 'kkeu-te'. And 끝 is only the noun 'the end' — to say something 'finishes/ends' you need the verb 끝나다 (영화가 끝났어요), not the bare noun. Handy collocations: 길 끝, 맨 끝, 끝까지.

Saying 길 끝 있어요 without 에. To place something at the end, mark location: 길 끝에 편의점이 있어요.

usage: 이·그·저·어느 + 쪽, written as one word
the right side / the left side
오른·왼 + 쪽 for left and right
examples: 화장실은 저쪽이에요.
The restroom is over that way.
저쪽이에요 = 'it's that way', a bare location answer
이쪽으로 쭉 가시면 출구가 나와요.
If you keep going this way, you'll reach the exit.
이쪽으로 = in this direction; 으로 with movement
죄송한데, 시청은 어느 쪽으로 가야 돼요?
Excuse me, which way do I go for City Hall?
어느 쪽으로 + 가야 돼요 = real 'which way' question
nuance: 쪽 is a native dependent noun meaning 'side / direction' and is the workhorse of everyday directions. It attaches to demonstratives (이쪽/그쪽/저쪽/어느 쪽) and to 오른/왼 (오른쪽, 왼쪽). The key contrast is 쪽 vs 방향 (方向): 쪽 is concrete and deictic — a side you can point at right here ('over there, this way') — while 방향 is the more abstract heading of travel ('the opposite direction', 'the right direction'); you point 이쪽 but you check 방향이 맞아요?. 쪽 can also politely mean 'your side/end' (그쪽 = 'you' softly). Register is neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: write 이쪽/저쪽/오른쪽 as ONE word (이 쪽 with a space is wrong), and use the direction particle 으로 for movement — 이쪽으로 가요 ('go this way'), not 이쪽에 가요 (에 marks a static spot, not a heading).

usage: 이·그·저 + 곳, written as one word
adjective + 곳; a frequent modifier pattern
에서 marks the spot of an action
examples: 여기는 유명한 곳이에요.
This is a famous place.
유명한 곳이에요 = 'it's a famous place', noun + 이에요
조용한 곳에서 좀 쉬고 싶어요.
I want to rest somewhere quiet.
곳에서 = at the place where you rest; action particle 에서
여행하면서 가 보고 싶은 곳을 미리 적어 뒀어요.
I wrote down in advance the places I want to visit on the trip.
가 보고 싶은 곳 = clause + 곳; 적어 두다 = note down for later
nuance: 곳 is a native dependent noun meaning 'place/spot', and it almost always rides on a modifier — an adjective or a relative clause (조용한 곳, 가 본 곳, 이곳). The near-synonym is 데, and the dividing line is register: 곳 is the slightly more formal, written-feeling word (you see it in guidebooks, reviews, signs), while 데 is the casual, spoken word. There is also a grammar difference — 곳 can pair with demonstratives to stand a bit more independently (이곳/그곳), whereas 데 leans even harder on a preceding modifier. Compare 위치 too: 위치 (位置) is the abstract coordinates 'where something sits', but 곳 is a place you go to or are in. Pronunciation pitfall: the final ㅅ is an unreleased 't' stop, so 곳 alone sounds like 'got' with the t held; before a vowel it surfaces, so 곳에 → 'go-se'. And don't drop the particle: say 곳에서 쉬어요, not 곳 쉬어요.

Dropping the particle. An action 'at a place' needs 에서: 조용한 곳에서 쉬어요, not 조용한 곳 쉬어요.
Using 곳 for abstract position. If you mean 'its location/position is good', use 위치 (위치가 좋아요), not 곳.

usage: V-(으)ㄹ + 데 = a place to do V
데 also = the part/spot (of the body) that…
another V-(으)ㄹ + 데 collocation travelers use
examples: 갈 데가 없어요.
I have no place to go.
갈 데 = a place to go; the modifier is obligatory
이 근처에 조용한 데 좀 아세요?
Do you know somewhere quiet around here?
조용한 데 = a quiet spot; casual, friendly ask
어디 아픈 데 있으면 말씀하세요.
If anywhere hurts, please tell me.
아픈 데 = the spot that hurts; 데 = the affected part
nuance: 데 is the casual, conversational dependent noun for 'place/spot', and it is grammatically bound: it can never stand alone the way 곳 sometimes can — it must follow a modifier (갈 데, 먹을 데, 조용한 데, 아픈 데). The contrast with 곳 is purely register and feel: in speech Koreans reach for 데 (갈 데 없어요), while writing, reviews, and formal signage prefer 곳 (방문할 곳). 데 also has a special sense English speakers love once they see it — 'the spot/part that…', as in 아픈 데 (the place that hurts) or 불편한 데 (the part that's uncomfortable), which 곳 does not naturally cover. The big trap is homonym confusion: this place-noun 데 is unrelated to the sentence connector -는데/-은데 ('and/but/background'), even though they look identical; 갈 데가 없어요 (noun) vs 가고 싶은데 표가 없어요 (connector). Keep a modifier in front and you'll always read it as the place-noun.

usage: 창가 = by the window; a top travel collocation
에 marks where you sit; pairs with 앉다
잡다 = secure a seat or spot
examples: 창가 자리로 주세요.
A window seat, please.
자리로 주세요 = 'give me the ~ seat'; 로 picks the option
여기 빈자리 있어요?
Is there an empty seat here?
빈자리 있어요? = the standard 'seat free here?' ask
일행이 자리 잡는 동안 제가 주문할게요.
While my group grabs a table, I'll order.
자리(를) 잡다 = secure seats; 동안 = 'during/while'
nuance: 자리 is the native everyday noun for a seat or a spot you occupy — a seat on a train, a table at a restaurant, a place in a line, even a 'position' in life (좋은 자리 = a good job/standing). The crucial contrast is 자리 vs 의자: 의자 (椅子) is the physical chair as an object, while 자리 is the seat/spot as a space you take or reserve — so you ask 자리 있어요? ('is there a seat/spot?'), not 의자 있어요? (which sounds like 'do you have a chair to sell?'). 자리 collocates richly: 창가 자리 (window seat), 빈자리 (empty seat), 자리에 앉다 (sit down), 자리를 잡다/맡다 (grab/save a spot), 자리를 비우다 (step away from one's seat). Register is neutral and friendly. English-speaker pitfall: with 앉다 ('sit') use the location particle 에 — 자리에 앉아요, not 자리 앉아요; and to choose a seat type use 로/으로 (창가 자리로).

Dropping 에 with 앉다. 'Sit in the seat' is 자리에 앉아요; 자리 앉아요 is missing the particle.
Using 있다 wrong for a free seat. Ask 빈자리 있어요? ('is there an empty seat?'); 자리가 비었어요? is also fine but means 'is the seat vacated?'.

usage: 에 marks the inside corner as a location
N + 구석 = the inside corner of N
구석 + 자리, a quiet nook seat
examples: 가방이 방 구석에 있어요.
The bag is in the corner of the room.
구석에 있어요 = sits in the inside corner; location 에
우리 구석 자리로 앉을까요?
Shall we sit at the corner table?
구석 자리 = a tucked-away corner seat; -ㄹ까요? suggests
청소하면서 집 구석구석을 다 닦았어요.
While cleaning I wiped every nook of the house.
구석구석 = thoroughly, all over; vivid native usage
nuance: 구석 is a native noun for an inside corner — the nook where two walls of a room or the inner edges of a box meet — and figuratively a tucked-away, out-of-the-way spot. The sharp contrast is 구석 vs 모퉁이: 모퉁이 is the OUTSIDE corner of a street or building, the bend you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다 = turn the corner), whereas 구석 is an INSIDE nook you tuck into; you can sit in a 구석 but you turn a 모퉁이. There is also the lovely reduplicated form 구석구석 ('every nook and cranny, thoroughly'). Register is neutral, slightly cozy/colloquial. Note 구석 can carry a faintly negative shade (a 'neglected back corner'), so a hotel 'corner room' marketed positively might be called 코너 instead. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 구석 for a street corner — that's 모퉁이; and keep the particle — 구석에 있어요 for location, 구석에서 for an action done there.

Dropping the particle. Location takes 에 (구석에 있어요); an action done there takes 에서 (구석에서 사진을 찍었어요).

usage: N + 속 = the interior/depths of N
examples: 가방 속에 여권이 있어요.
My passport is inside the bag.
가방 속에 = down inside the bag; location 에
주머니 속에서 동전을 찾았어요.
I found a coin inside my pocket.
속에서 = inside (where the finding happened); action 에서
사진 속 그 골목이 아직도 기억나요.
I still remember that alley in the photo.
사진 속 = within the picture; figurative 속
nuance: 속 is a native noun for the inside, interior, or depths of something — especially a filled, enclosed, or three-dimensional thing (가방 속, 물속, 숲속), and figuratively the inside of an image or a heart (사진 속, 마음속 = deep in one's heart). The essential contrast is 속 vs 안: 안 marks being within a boundary or enclosure (방 안 = inside the room, 건물 안 = inside the building), neutral and structural, while 속 stresses being embedded in the substance or down in the depths (물속 = under the water, 가방 속 = buried in the bag). So 방 안 is natural but 방 속 sounds odd; 물속 is natural but 물 안 sounds odd. 속 also has bodily/emotional senses (속이 안 좋다 = upset stomach; 속상하다 = heartsick) that 안 lacks. Register neutral. English-speaker pitfall: don't reflexively map 'inside' to whichever you learned first — use 안 for rooms/buildings/bounded areas and 속 for filled or deep spaces; and keep 에: 가방 속에 있어요.

usage: 으로 = toward outside; pairs with 나가다
common collocation: 바깥 공기 좀 쐬다
examples: 바깥에 사람이 많아요.
There are many people outside.
바깥에 = outside as a location; existence 에
바깥 날씨가 생각보다 추워요.
The weather outside is colder than expected.
바깥 날씨 = the outdoor weather; 생각보다 = 'than I thought'
바람도 쐴 겸 바깥으로 잠깐 나갈까요?
Shall we step outside for a bit to get some air?
바깥으로 나가다 = go out; -ㄹ 겸 = 'also so as to…'
nuance: 바깥 is a native noun meaning the outside / the outdoors, the natural opposite of 안 (inside). Its near-synonym is 밖: the two are largely interchangeable for 'outside' (바깥에/밖에, 바깥 날씨/바깥 = 'out there'), but 바깥 feels a touch more concrete and substantial — 'the outdoors as a place' — while 밖 is the lighter, more frequent 'outside' and also forms compounds like 창밖 (outside the window) and 문밖 (outside the door). Be very careful: the string 밖에 doubles as the grammar particle '밖에' meaning 'only/nothing but' (천 원밖에 없어요 = 'I have only 1,000 won'), so when you want the location 'outside' it is safer and clearer to say 바깥에. Register is neutral; there's also a dated sense 바깥양반/바깥일 ('the husband / outside affairs'). English-speaker pitfalls: spell it with final ㅌ — 바깥 (not 바깟/바같), and that ㅌ links to vowels so 바깥에 sounds like 'ba-kka-te'; for going out use direction 으로 (바깥으로 나가요).

usage: 에 marks the location on both sides
N + 양쪽 = the two sides of N
양쪽 + 끝 = the two far ends
examples: 길 양쪽에 가게가 있어요.
There are shops on both sides of the road.
양쪽에 = on both sides; location 에
저는 양쪽 다 괜찮아요.
Either one is fine with me.
양쪽 다 = both/either; common when choosing
다리 양쪽 끝에 경비가 서 있더라고요.
There were guards standing at both ends of the bridge.
양쪽 끝 = the two far ends; -더라고요 = 'I noticed that…'
nuance: 양쪽 is 양 (兩 'two/both', the Sino-Korean root also in 양손 'both hands', 양면 'both sides') plus the native 쪽 ('side'), literally 'both sides'. It names the two opposing sides of something — a road, a door, a choice between two options. Compare 양쪽 vs 양옆: 양쪽 is the general 'both sides', while 양옆 specifically means 'both flanks / the two sides beside' something (양옆에 앉다 = sit on either side of). And contrast it with 둘 다 / 양쪽 다 ('both of them' when choosing): 양쪽 다 괜찮아요 = 'either is fine'. Register neutral. English-speaker pitfalls: it is built from the bound root 양, not from a counting word, so 'both sides' is 양쪽, never 둘쪽 or 두 쪽 (두 쪽 would mean 'two pieces/slices'); and because 양 inherently means exactly two, do not use 양쪽 for three or more sides — for 'all sides/all around' use 사방 (四方) or 곳곳. Keep the particle: 양쪽에 for location.

usage: 가 + adjective; reviews love this phrase
를 marks the location you verify
를 + 보내다; share location in a chat
examples: 호텔 위치가 정말 좋아요.
The hotel's location is really good.
위치가 좋다 = good location; the classic review line
지도에서 위치를 다시 확인했어요.
I double-checked the location on the map.
위치를 확인하다 = verify a position; 에서 = on the map
지금 제 위치 보내 드릴 테니까 그쪽으로 와 주세요.
I'll send you my location now, so please come there.
위치를 보내다 = share location; -ㄹ 테니까 = 'I'll…, so…'
nuance: 위치 is Sino-Korean 位置 (位 'position/rank' + 置 'to place'), literally 'where something is set' — the abstract location or position of a thing. It is the natural word in maps, GPS, apps, and reviews: 위치가 좋다 (good location), 현재 위치 (current location), 위치를 공유하다/보내다 (share/send location). The key contrast is 위치 vs 곳/데: 곳 and 데 are 'a place you go to or are in' (조용한 곳, 갈 데), whereas 위치 is the coordinate/position 'where it sits' relative to other things — you don't 'go to a 위치', you check or describe one. Compare also 장소 (場所), which is a concrete venue/site for an event (모임 장소 = meeting place); 위치 is more abstract than 장소. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in writing and signage. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 위치 to mean 'a nice place to visit' — say 곳/데; and pronounce 치 as 'chi' (위치 = 'wi-chi'), not 'wi-ti'.

usage: 어느 + 방향 for asking a heading
examples: 이 방향이 맞아요?
Is this the right direction?
방향이 맞다 = the heading is correct; basic check
반대 방향으로 가는 버스를 탔어요.
I took a bus going the opposite direction.
반대 방향으로 = the opposite way; 으로 with 가다
서울역은 지금 어느 방향으로 가야 하는지 잘 모르겠어요.
I'm not sure which direction I should head for Seoul Station.
어느 방향으로 가야 하다 = which way to head; real lost-traveler line
nuance: 방향 is Sino-Korean 方向 (方 'direction/region' + 向 'to face/head toward'), the abstract heading or orientation of movement. The central contrast is 방향 vs 쪽: 쪽 is the concrete, point-at-it 'side/way' right in front of you (이쪽, 저쪽, 오른쪽), while 방향 is the abstract course of travel you reason about — 'the opposite direction', 'the right direction', 'which way leads there'. So you point 이쪽 ('this way, here') but you verify 방향이 맞아요? ('am I heading right?') and warn 반대 방향이에요 ('that's the wrong way'). Compare 위치 too: 위치 is where something is (static position), 방향 is which way it faces or you move. Register neutral, fine in speech and signs (e.g., 부산 방향 on a road sign = 'toward Busan'). English-speaker pitfalls: for movement use 으로 (반대 방향으로 가요), not 에 (방향에 가요 is wrong); and don't confuse 방향 with the look-alike 방학 (school vacation) — same 방, unrelated meanings.

usage: at the front, directly in front
N + 정면 = the front face of N
에서 = the front as where an action happens
examples: 건물 정면에 큰 문이 있어요.
There's a big door at the front of the building.
정면에 = on the front face; location 에
여기서 정면으로 쭉 가시면 돼요.
Just go straight ahead from here.
정면으로 쭉 가다 = head straight on; direction 으로
역 정면에서 만나는 게 제일 찾기 쉬울 것 같아요.
Meeting right in front of the station seems easiest to find.
정면에서 만나다 = meet at the front; 에서 for the meeting spot
nuance: 정면 is Sino-Korean 正面 (正 'straight/correct' + 面 'face/surface'), literally 'the straight face' — the front-facing side of something or the space directly ahead of you. The key contrast is 정면 vs 앞: 앞 is the general, everyday 'front / in front of' (집 앞 = in front of the house) and is what casual speech uses; 정면 is more specific and emphatic, the face that looks straight at you or the line dead-ahead — a building's façade (건물 정면) or 'straight in front' (정면으로 가다). So everyday 'in front of me' is 제 앞, but 'the front of the building / head-on' is where 정면 shines. It also appears in 정면충돌 (head-on collision) and 정면으로 보다 (face head-on). Register neutral-to-formal. English-speaker pitfalls: don't reach for 정면 in casual 'in front of' situations — use 앞; and keep particles straight — 정면에 for a static location, 정면으로 for the straight-ahead direction, 정면에서 for an action done at the front.

usage: 에 marks the rim as a location
N + 가장자리 = the outer rim of N
으로 = in the direction of the rim
examples: 탁자 가장자리에 컵을 놓았어요.
I set the cup at the edge of the table.
가장자리에 = on the rim; location 에
호수 가장자리를 따라 천천히 걸었어요.
I walked slowly along the edge of the lake.
가장자리를 따라 걷다 = walk along the rim
컵을 가장자리에 너무 가까이 두면 떨어질 수도 있어요.
If you leave the cup too close to the edge, it might fall.
가장자리에 가까이 = close to the rim; -ㄹ 수도 있다 = 'might'
nuance: 가장자리 is a native noun for the outer edge or rim of a flat or bounded thing — a table, a page, a lake, a field. It contrasts sharply with three neighbors: 끝 is the end/tip of something long or linear (길 끝 = the road's end), 구석 is an inside corner where two walls meet (방 구석), and 모퉁이 is the outside corner of a street you turn at (모퉁이를 돌다) — so a tabletop has a 가장자리 (rim) but a hallway has a 끝 (end) and a room has a 구석 (nook). A close synonym is 끄트머리 ('the very edge/tip', more colloquial), and 테두리 means specifically a border/frame line around something. Register is neutral, everyday. English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 가장자리 for the end of a road or hallway (that's 끝), and don't confuse the noun 가장자리 (edge) with the unrelated superlative adverb 가장 ('most / -est', as in 가장 큰 = biggest) — they merely share the first two syllables. Keep the particle: 가장자리에 for location, 가장자리를 따라 for 'along'.
